## This tutorial

<img src="https://i.giphy.com/media/v1.Y2lkPTc5MGI3NjExeDFidmtrcTJhenU1NGRtdXA5N292Ynp3Y3BxcHRhYjR2MnowOGJ0ZiZlcD12MV9pbnRlcm5hbF9naWZfYnlfaWQmY3Q9Zw/djRJNZqj508sE/giphy.gif" alt="gif of deadpool greeting" width = "900"/>

Within a network, nodes and ties vary.
But how much do they vary and are there associations in this variance?
By the end of this tutorial, you will be able to:

- [ ] &nbsp; measure the richness of a network in terms of attribute types
- [ ] &nbsp; measure how diverse a network is
- [ ] &nbsp; measure how heterophilous the ties in a network are
- [ ] &nbsp; test how heterophilous the ties in a network are compared to random networks
- [ ] &nbsp; test how heterophilous the ties in a network are compared to permutations of the original network
- [ ] &nbsp; regress a network's ties on nodal and dyadic attributes
- [ ] &nbsp; choose which categories of an attribute enter a regression
- [ ] &nbsp; account for differences among senders and receivers with fixed effects or random intercepts
- [ ] &nbsp; regress one layer of a network on other layers, including in a cognitive social structure
- [ ] &nbsp; move a regression's formula to another model, and check what it keeps

## Initial visualisation

For this session, we'll explore a couple of different datasets.
First, let's examine homogeneity/`r gloss("heterogeneity")` in the Marvel dataset from `{manynet}`,
`fict_marvel`.
The dataset is quite complicated,
so to make this simpler, let's concentrate on:

- just the relationships part of the network
- just the positive (friendship) ties and not the negative (enmity) ties
- the main (giant) component without any isolates
- just those characters that appear in the comics more than average

Fortunately, all these data cleaning moves are easy to do in `{manynet}`,
and can be seen in the following chunk in order:


This gives us an `r gloss("undirected")` network of nearly twenty characters and a little more than 100 edges.
Recall that this data has several nodal attributes.
Let's explore a couple of these attributes, "Gender" and "PowerOrigin", visually
using `graphr()`.


These variables seem to be distributed unevenly across the network.
There seems to be some `r gloss("homophily")` -- or like choosing like --
operating here, but it is difficult to say conclusively because there are
clearly more male than female superheros,
as well as clearly more superheros of mutant origin than others.
So what might seem like homophily could just be a result of there being
many more opportunities for ties between nodes of some categories.
We therefore need to establish how diverse this network really is.

## Measuring richness

Some categorical variables have more categories than others,
and this can be thought of as indicating greater diversity than e.g. a binary
categorical variable.
A measure of this 'richness' is inherited from the study of biodiversity.
`r gloss("Richness","richness")` calculates the number of different categories that appear in
the data for a given variable.
Let's calculate the richness of all of the variables in our Marvel data.

```{r rich, purl = FALSE}
net_node_attributes(marvel_friends)
```


::: {.callout}
<span class="callout-label">**Try it yourself**:</span> This section includes an interactive quiz in the live tutorial — run `run_tute()` at the R console to try it.
:::

Note though that 'richness' as a network measure does not include 
any sense of how distributed these categories are around the network.
There is a measure of nodal richness available,
which counts the number of different categories to which each node is tied,
but this does not offer a summary of how evenly distributed the appearance
of categories are.
For that we would need to move on to something like the Blau index.

## Measuring diversity

Another measure that reflects the diversity or `r gloss("heterogeneity")` in the 
network for each attribute is the Blau Index.
Recall that the Blau index for any given variable is:

$$1 - \sum p_i^2$$

where $p_i$ represents the proportion of observations holding $i$, 
which indexes each of the given categories.
A perfectly homogeneous group (all the same category) would receive a score of 0,
while a perfectly `r gloss("heterogeneous","heterogeneity")` group (with members spread evenly over the maximum categories)
would receive a score of 1.
Obtain the network diversity scores for the five attributes used above.


Looks like there is more diversity in terms of where these characters got
their powers, whether they have significant intellectual powers,
and their gender, than their attractiveness or their wealth.

We can also cross-reference this diversity.
For example, we might be interested in whether our comic book heroes
are equally gender diverse across their (power) origin stories,
or equally intellectually diverse across gender.^[Note that this works for calculated categorical variables too, such as cluster/group assignment from community detection or equivalence classes.]


`to_subgraphs()` splits the network into one subgraph for each category,
so the length of the vector returned as a result
is the number of categories in the attribute that is split on.
It looks like some origin stories are more gender diverse than others.
Gods (just Thor here) and humans are all men,
whereas those with mutant or radiation origin stories are more gender diverse.
There doesn't appear to be much difference in intellect 
across gender categories in this data.

Ok, this tells us about how (un)even the distribution of these variables is in this network,
but it doesn't necessarily tell us whether ties are appearing more frequently
_between_ nodes of similar (or different) categories.
For that we need to look at `r gloss("homophily")`/`r gloss("heterophily.", "heterophily")`

## Measuring heterophily

The EI (or E-I) index offers a way to measure the degree to which ties
appear between rather than within groups of nodes of the same category.
Recall that the EI index is calculated as:

$$\frac{E-I}{E+I}$$

where $E$ is the number of ties present between a variable's categories (i.e. external),
and $I$ is the number of ties present within a variable's categories (i.e. internal).
As such, an EI index of -1 suggests perfect homophily, whereas an EI index of +1 suggests perfect `r gloss("heterophily.","heterophily")`
(This is why the function is called `net_by_heterophily()`).

Check how homophilic three variables in the network are,
"Gender", "PowerOrigin", and "Attractive".
Please assign the results so that we can use them later.


::: {.callout}
<span class="callout-label">**Try it yourself**:</span> This section includes an interactive quiz in the live tutorial — run `run_tute()` at the R console to try it.
:::

Ultimately though, these are just scores,
and doesn't tell us whether this is any more or less than
what we might expect the score to be by chance for a network
of this size and density and distribution of that attribute.

## CUG tests

To see whether we should be surprised by scores this high/low, 
we compare these scores with those from a series of `r gloss("random graphs","random")`
(Erdös-Renyi/Bernoulli) of the same dimensions and
distribution of the attribute.
This can help us establish whether there is
more homophily or heterophily than expected by chance.

This is often called a `r gloss("conditional uniform graph","cug")` or CUG test,
but `{infernet}` uses more descriptive function names,
such as `test_random()`.
Plot the results of running this function with respect to the EI index on each of the three variables.
These plots can be made if you have `{autograph}` installed and loaded.
You can specify that five hundred simulations should be used using `times = 500`.


The plots of these results use a dotted vertical line for 0 where this is in bounds,
a red vertical line for the observed score,
and a density plot of the scores from the randomly generated networks.
The grey tails of the distribution are a visual aid indicating the most extreme 5% of scores
from the distribution.
The results are _really_ interesting.

<img src="https://i.giphy.com/media/v1.Y2lkPTc5MGI3NjExNzlsM3J1dm9tb2tlYjB4bGw0cGxuc3RodXpvdjNhcGJ5cXV2MndjbiZlcD12MV9pbnRlcm5hbF9naWZfYnlfaWQmY3Q9Zw/AbYxDs20DECQw/giphy.gif" alt="gif of ironman explosion" width = "900"/>

Despite being the larger coefficients (in absolute terms),
it looks like we cannot reject the null hypothesis that there is no homophily
for gender nor for attractiveness.
Both observed scores fall within the range of scores we would expect from
randomly generated networks with the same distribution of that variable.

However, we can reject the null hypothesis with respect to their power origin story.
While the coefficient itself is close to 0 (neither strong homophily nor heterophily),
all the random networks generated returned larger EI scores, between .1 and .4.

::: {.callout}
<span class="callout-label">**Try it yourself**:</span> This section includes an interactive quiz in the live tutorial — run `run_tute()` at the R console to try it.
:::

## QAP tests

Ah, but perhaps random graphs are not the best reference group 
for establishing whether there is a significant homophily effect here.
After all, social networks are not completely random; 
they are _structured_ in particular ways, such as some nodes having higher degrees
than others, or there being a `r gloss("core and periphery","core")` or `r gloss("community")` topology.

Another approach to establishing a baseline for whether we should be surprised
by a given score or not is to use `r gloss("permutations","permutation")` of the underlying network
instead of random graphs.
Permuting the network retains the structure of the network
because the ties are kept and only the labels (variables) are reassigned randomly.
Let's first plot the observed data and some permuted data next to each other.


::: {.callout}
<span class="callout-label">**Try it yourself**:</span> This section includes an interactive quiz in the live tutorial — run `run_tute()` at the R console to try it.
:::

This single permutation suggests a more even mixing of these
attributes is possible, but it is just a single permutation.
Let's try a `r gloss("QAP","qap")` test that runs this over a succession of permutations,
just as we did with random graphs.
Plot the results for gender and power according to the random and permutation baselines.


Again, we see that there is perhaps nothing so surprising that we got the homophily score
for gender that we did, but the lack of power origin heterophily is surprising.
Note how the distributions are generally wider when permuting the observed network 
than creating a random distribution (be mindful of the scale of the _x_-axis).
That is, taking into account the structure of the network leads us to
expect a larger spread in the EI index than when the variable is distributed across a random network.

::: {.callout}
<span class="callout-label">**Try it yourself**:</span> This section includes an interactive quiz in the live tutorial — run `run_tute()` at the R console to try it.
:::

CUG and QAP tests are useful for establishing whether there is
more or less homophily than expected by chance,
with QAP tests being more conservative and better taking into account the structure of the network.
Alternative reference networks can also be used that condition on more structural
information than completely random graphs, 
but introduce potentially more variation in the network structure than permutations.
These include for example `r gloss("configuration")` networks that retain the degree distribution observed in the original network, but could result in varying clustering,
or networks that are conditioned on the dyad census (i.e. `r gloss("MAN","man")` models).
And yet none of these approaches allow us to examine multiple variables at once
or control for other factors.
For that we need to move on to network regression.

## Network regression

Next let us examine homophily in another network.
The data were collected as part of an early experiment on communication between social network researchers who were using an Electronic Information Exchange System (EIES).
You may recognise some of the names.
The main network consists of 32 scholars with directed ties weighted by the total number of messages sent from $i$ to $j$ over the period of the study.
Nodal attributes collected include the primary discipline and number of citations in the social science citation index at the start of the study.

```{r introeies, purl = FALSE, fig.width=9}
ison_networkers
graphr(ison_networkers, node_color = "Discipline")
```

Let's use both the continuous `Citations` and the categorical `Discipline` variables
and come up with a couple of key hypotheses:

- $H_1$: researchers send more emails to those who are cited more (popularity hypothesis)
- $H_2$: researchers send more emails to those of the same discipline (disciplinary homophily hypothesis)

`estimate_mrqap()` fits a `r gloss("MRQAP","mrqap")` model from a formula.
The left-hand side names the ties to explain, here the `weight` of each tie,
and the right-hand side lists the terms that might explain them:

- `ego(Citations)` and `alter(Citations)` are the sender's and the receiver's citations.
  Because this network is `r gloss("directed")`, both `r gloss("ego")` and `r gloss("alter")` effects make sense.
  $H_1$ is about the alter effect.
- `diff(Citations)` is the absolute difference between the sender's and the receiver's citations.
  `diff(Citations, transformer_fn = identity)` gives the signed difference instead.
- `ego(Discipline)` and `alter(Discipline)` are the sender's and the receiver's discipline.
  A categorical attribute gets one 0/1 column for each category,
  less the first category (here Anthropology), which is the reference.
- `same(Discipline)` is 1 where the sender and the receiver share a discipline.
  This is $H_2$.

Let's start with a model of all five terms for each attribute.
Homophily is only interpretable net of the effects it contains,
since two researchers who are both highly cited are alike, but each is also highly cited.
We are using `times = 200` here so that the model runs quickly in this tutorial,
but for publication quality results you would want to base your conclusions on 2000
permutations or more.


By default, the printing method for this model includes the key information you might need.
We can also use tidy methods to obtain just the table of coefficients (e.g. `tidy()`)
or the model summary statistics (e.g. `glance()`).
`{autograph}` also includes a plot method for these results to
facilitate the quick interpretation of these results,
and as long as this is loaded you can simply call `plot()` on the model object.


This violin plot presents the distribution of the test statistic for each coefficient
across the `r gloss("permutations","permutation")` of the network,
with the statistic fitted from the data as a red dot.
Lines inside each violin mark the 95% thresholds.
A red dot outside those lines is one that the permutations rarely reach.

::: {.callout}
<span class="callout-label">**Try it yourself**:</span> This section includes an interactive quiz in the live tutorial — run `run_tute()` at the R console to try it.
:::

## Categories

`same(Discipline)` gives one coefficient for all disciplines,
so it assumes that sociologists are as homophilous as anthropologists.
That need not be so.
Two terms split a categorical attribute further:

- `same(Discipline, diff = TRUE)` gives one 0/1 column for each discipline,
  1 where the sender and the receiver both hold it.
- `mix(Discipline)` gives one 0/1 column for each pair of a sender's and a receiver's discipline,
  such as sociologist to anthropologist,
  less the first pair as the reference.

With four disciplines, `mix()` can quickly use up a small network.
`levels =` chooses which categories (or pairs) get a column.
Give their names, as they appear in the results,
such as `levels = "Sociology"` or, for `mix()`, `levels = "Sociology -> Anthropology"`.
The categories that are left out become the reference together.

Fit a model with the citation terms,
discipline homophily for each discipline,
and the two mixing terms between sociologists and anthropologists, in both directions.


Now see how `levels =` changes the reference category of `ego()` and `alter()`.
Fit a model that asks only whether sociologists send or receive more messages
than everyone else, and whether researchers of the same discipline message each other more.


::: {.callout}
<span class="callout-label">**Try it yourself**:</span> This section includes an interactive quiz in the live tutorial — run `run_tute()` at the R console to try it.
:::

## Sender and receiver effects

Some researchers send many more messages than others,
and some receive many more.
The ties of one sender are then not independent of one another,
and a model that ignores this may mistake a busy sender for an effect of their attributes.
There are two ways to account for each node's own level of activity and popularity.

**Fixed effects** absorb a separate intercept for each sender and each receiver.
Write them after a bare bar at the end of the formula, as in `{fixest}`:
`| sender + receiver`.
Because these intercepts absorb everything about a sender or a receiver,
a term that does not vary within them, such as `ego(Citations)` or `alter(Discipline)`,
cannot be estimated, and the model stops and names it.
Only the dyadic terms, which vary within each sender and receiver, can stay.
The model then reports a 'within' R-squared,
the share of the variance within senders and receivers that it explains.

Fit a model of citation difference and discipline homophily with sender and receiver fixed effects.


**Random intercepts** instead treat each sender's and each receiver's intercept
as drawn from a normal distribution, as in `{lme4}`.
Write each one in parentheses: `(1 | sender) + (1 | receiver)`.
Random intercepts keep the nodal terms in the model,
but each permutation now fits a mixed model, which takes longer.
Here we use `times = 100`.


::: {.callout}
<span class="callout-label">**Try it yourself**:</span> This section includes an interactive quiz in the live tutorial — run `run_tute()` at the R console to try it.
:::

## Model controls

So far each model has used its default controls.
`control_mrqap()` shows them all, and checks any that you change.
Its result goes to the `control =` argument of `estimate_mrqap()`.
The most useful controls are:

- `family`: `"auto"` reads it from the outcome (`"binomial"` for a binary outcome, otherwise `"gaussian"`).
  The message counts here might also be fitted as `"poisson"` or `"negbin"`.
- `permute`: `"predictor"` (Dekker's double semi-partialling, the default) or `"outcome"`.
- `seed`: a number, so that the same permutations, and so the same p-values, come back each time.
- `ncores`: the number of cores to run the permutations on.

Look at the controls, then fit a model with a seed, twice.


Running in parallel only pays where each permutation is costly:
a family other than gaussian, random intercepts, or a cognitive social structure (see the next section),
on a network of more than about 50 nodes, with 1,000 or more permutations.
Elsewhere, starting the workers costs more time than it saves.
For such a model, outside this tutorial, you would write, for example:

```r
estimate_mrqap(advice ~ tie(friends) + same(dept) + (1 | reporter),
               ison_hightech, times = 2000,
               control = control_mrqap(ncores = 2, seed = 1234))
```

::: {.callout}
<span class="callout-label">**Try it yourself**:</span> This section includes an interactive quiz in the live tutorial — run `run_tute()` at the R console to try it.
:::

## Layers and perceptions

The networks so far have had one kind of tie.
A `r gloss("multiplex")` network has several, called layers,
and one layer can explain another.
`ison_hightech` holds Krackhardt's (1987) data on 21 managers of a high-tech company.
Every manager reported who goes to whom for advice, and who is friends with whom.
Each of those layers is a cognitive social structure (CSS):
21 reports of the whole network, one from each manager.
The `reports` layer is the formal reporting structure, which is the same for everyone.

```{r introtech, purl = FALSE}
ison_hightech
```

`estimate_mrqap()` detects a CSS and fits every reported `r gloss("dyad")`,
one for each sender, receiver, and reporter: 21 x 20 x 21 = 8,820 observations.
A permutation relabels senders, receivers, and reporters together.
These terms read another layer:

- `tie(friends)` is whether the sender is friends with the receiver,
  in the same reporter's report, since `friends` is a CSS layer too.
- `exchange(friends)` is the reverse tie, whether the receiver is friends with the sender.
- `indeg(reports, node = "ego")` is the sender's indegree in the reporting structure,
  that is, how many managers report to them.
  `node = "alter"` would read the receiver's instead.

A term must not read the outcome's own ties,
since permuting the outcome would not permute such a predictor with it.
So `tie(advice)` would stop with an error.

Fit a model of advice on friendship, reciprocated friendship,
the sender's number of reports, and being in the same department.
Advice ties are binary, so this is a logistic model of 8,820 observations,
and we use `times = 50` with a seed.


A report about one's own ties can differ from a report about the ties of others.
The reporter terms describe who made each report:

- `reporter(level)` is the reporter's level in the hierarchy, the same over their whole report.
- `reporter_ego` is 1 where the reporter is the sender,
  that is, in a report about whom the reporter goes to for advice.
- `reporter_alter` is 1 where the reporter is the receiver.

Add the reporter's level and `reporter_ego` to the model.


Each manager may also simply report more or fewer ties overall.
`(1 | reporter)` adds a random intercept for each reporter,
and `| reporter` a fixed effect, which absorbs `reporter(level)`.
On a CSS, each permutation of such a model takes much longer,
so try these outside the tutorial, with `ncores = 2` and more permutations.

::: {.callout}

## Moving a formula

The same formula can describe other models of the same network.
`specify_ergm()` rewrites an MRQAP formula for `{ergm}`,
and `specify_dynam()` for a `{goldfish}` DyNAM.
Each term that has an equivalent is rewritten,
such as `diff(Citations)` as `absdiff("Citations")`
and a `| sender` fixed effect as ergm's `sender` term,
and each term that the other model cannot fit is dropped and named.
Give the network as well,
so that a categorical attribute is written as a categorical term.
`tidy()` of the result has one row for each term,
with what the other model makes of it.

Rewrite a model of `ison_networkers` for ergm, and check each term.
Then do the same, without the network, for a model of `ison_hightech`.


The result is an ordinary formula,
so `ergm::ergm()` could fit it as it is.
We do not fit it here,
since an ERGM takes longer to estimate than this tutorial allows,
and an ERGM of the message counts would need a valued ERGM.

## Free play

While these are the conclusions from this 'play' data,
you may have more and more interesting data at hand.
How would you go about specifying such a model?
Why is such an approach more appropriate for network data than linear
or logistic regression?

If you want another network to try,
`ison_lawfirm` holds Lazega's data on the advice, friendship, and cowork ties
among 71 lawyers, with their status, gender, office, practice, and seniority.
Does advice follow friendship, office, or practice?
Which terms would you hold fixed for each sender?
